title: Buying a Coffee
contextVi: Một khách hàng gọi cà phê và bánh sandwich ở quán cà phê.

script.speaker: Waiter
script.text: Good morning. What would you like?

script.speaker: Mia
script.text: Good morning. A coffee, please.

script.speaker: Waiter
script.text: Large or small?

script.speaker: Mia
script.text: Small, please. With milk, but no sugar.

script.speaker: Waiter
script.text: Would you like anything to eat? We have cake and sandwiches.

script.speaker: Mia
script.text: A sandwich, please. Cheese, not chicken.

script.speaker: Waiter
script.text: Sure. That's three pounds fifty for the coffee and two pounds for the sandwich. So, five pounds fifty.

script.speaker: Mia
script.text: Here you are. Ten pounds.

script.speaker: Waiter
script.text: Thank you. Your change is four pounds fifty. Please sit down, and I will bring everything to your table.

script.speaker: Mia
script.text: Thank you. Excuse me, where is the toilet?

script.speaker: Waiter
script.text: It's next to the door, on the left.

script.speaker: Mia
script.text: Thank you very much.

questions.q: What size coffee does Mia order?
questions.explain: Mia nói: 'Small, please.'

questions.q: Which sandwich does Mia want?
questions.explain: 'Cheese, not chicken.' - phô mai, không phải gà.

questions.q: The total price is ____ pounds.
questions.explain: Ly cà phê 3.50 cộng sandwich 2.00 = 5.50 bảng.

questions.q: Mia's change is ____ pounds.
questions.explain: 'Your change is four pounds fifty.'

questions.q: Does Mia want sugar in her coffee?
questions.explain: 'With milk, but no sugar.'

questions.q: Where is the toilet?
options: Next to the door, on the left
questions.explain: 'It's next to the door, on the left.'

title: Meeting a New Neighbour
contextVi: Hai người hàng xóm làm quen và nói về công việc, gia đình.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Hello! I'm Ben. I live in flat number twelve.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Hi, Ben. I'm Sara. I'm your new neighbour. I live in flat number fourteen.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Nice to meet you. Where are you from?

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: I'm from Spain, but I work here in London. I'm a nurse.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: That's interesting. I'm a teacher. I teach music at a school near here.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Oh, I love music! I play the guitar.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Really? I play the piano. Do you have any brothers or sisters?

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Yes, I have one sister. She's twenty-two years old. She lives in Madrid.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Is Madrid a nice city?

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Yes, it's big and very sunny. Is there a supermarket near here?

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Yes, there is one at the end of the street. It opens at eight o'clock.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Great. Thanks, Ben. See you soon!

questions.q: What is Ben's flat number?
questions.explain: Ben: 'flat number twelve'; Sara ở số fourteen.

questions.q: What is Sara's job?
questions.explain: Sara: 'I'm a nurse.'

questions.q: What does Ben teach?
questions.explain: Ben: 'I teach music at a school near here.'

questions.q: Which instrument does Sara play?
questions.explain: Sara: 'I play the guitar.' (Ben chơi piano).

questions.q: Sara's sister is ____ years old.
questions.explain: 'She's twenty-two years old.'

questions.q: The supermarket opens at ____ o'clock.
questions.explain: 'It opens at eight o'clock.'

title: At the Train Station
contextVi: Một hành khách mua vé tàu đi Oxford ở quầy bán vé.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Good afternoon. Can I help you?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Yes, please. I'd like a ticket to Oxford.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Single or return?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Return, please. I come back tomorrow.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: That's eighteen pounds.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Can I pay by card?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Yes, of course. The next train leaves at two forty, from platform three.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Two forty, platform three. Is that right?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Yes, that's right. The journey takes one hour.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Thank you. And is there a café at the station?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Yes, it's opposite the ticket office.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Great. Thanks. Goodbye.

questions.q: What kind of ticket does the woman buy?
questions.explain: 'Return, please. I come back tomorrow.'

questions.q: The ticket costs ____ pounds.
questions.explain: 'That's eighteen pounds.'

questions.q: How does she pay?
questions.explain: 'Can I pay by card?' - 'Yes, of course.'

questions.q: What time does the train leave?
questions.explain: 'The next train leaves at two forty.'

questions.q: The train leaves from platform ____.
questions.explain: 'from platform three'.

questions.q: Where is the café?
questions.explain: 'it's opposite the ticket office.'

title: Plans for Saturday
contextVi: Hai người bạn lên kế hoạch đi biển vào cuối tuần.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Hi, Tom. What are you doing on Saturday?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Nothing special. Why?

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: Let's go to the beach. The weather is going to be hot.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Good idea. But I don't have a car.

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: No problem. My brother has a car. He can take us.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Great. What time shall we meet?

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: At nine o'clock, at my house.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Nine is a bit early. Can we meet at ten?

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: OK, ten o'clock is fine. Please bring some water and a hat.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Sure. Shall I bring some food too?

script.speaker: Lucy
script.text: No, I will make sandwiches. And in the evening, we can have dinner in a restaurant.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Perfect. See you on Saturday!

questions.q: Where are Lucy and Tom going on Saturday?
questions.explain: Lucy: 'Let's go to the beach.'

questions.q: What will the weather be like?
questions.explain: 'The weather is going to be hot.'

questions.q: How will they travel?
questions.explain: Tom không có xe; 'My brother has a car. He can take us.'

questions.q: What time will they meet?
questions.explain: Lucy đề nghị chín giờ, nhưng Tom xin muộn hơn và Lucy đồng ý: 'ten o'clock is fine'.

questions.q: Tom must bring some water and a ____.
questions.explain: 'Please bring some water and a hat.'

questions.q: Lucy will make ____.
questions.explain: 'No, I will make sandwiches.'

title: Booking a Doctor's Appointment
contextVi: Một bệnh nhân gọi điện đặt lịch khám với bác sĩ.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Good morning, Greenfield Medical Centre. How can I help you?

script.speaker: Patient
script.text: Hello. I'd like to make an appointment with Doctor Evans, please. I've had a bad cough for a week.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Let me see. Doctor Evans is free on Tuesday at ten thirty, or on Wednesday at four o'clock.

script.speaker: Patient
script.text: I work until five on Wednesday. Can I come on Tuesday?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, Tuesday at ten thirty is fine. Can I have your name, please?

script.speaker: Patient
script.text: It's Daniel Carter. That's C-A-R-T-E-R.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Thank you. And your date of birth?

script.speaker: Patient
script.text: The fourteenth of March, nineteen ninety-two.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Thank you. Please arrive fifteen minutes early to fill in a form, and bring your health card.

script.speaker: Patient
script.text: Sorry, did you say fifteen minutes?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Oh, no, sorry. Ten minutes is enough.

script.speaker: Patient
script.text: Ten minutes, and my health card. Thank you. Goodbye.

questions.q: What is the patient's problem?
questions.explain: 'I've had a bad cough for a week.'

questions.q: Which day is the appointment?
questions.explain: Bệnh nhân làm việc đến năm giờ thứ Tư nên chọn Tuesday.

questions.q: The appointment is at ____ (time).
questions.explain: 'Tuesday at ten thirty is fine.'

questions.q: The patient's surname is C-A-R-T-E-R, so it is ____.
questions.explain: Ghép các chữ cái C-A-R-T-E-R thành 'Carter'.

questions.q: The patient must arrive ____ minutes early.
questions.explain: Lễ tân nói 'fifteen' rồi sửa lại: 'Ten minutes is enough.'

questions.q: What must the patient bring?
questions.explain: 'bring your health card'.

title: Buying a Jacket
contextVi: Một người cha mua áo khoác cho con trai trong cửa hàng quần áo.

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: Hello, can I help you?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Yes, I'm looking for a jacket for my son. He's fourteen.

script.speaker: Assistant
script.text: What size is he?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: I think he's medium, but he's very tall, so maybe large.

script.speaker: Assistant

script.speaker: Customer

script.speaker: Assistant

script.text: Forty-five. That's good. Does it have a hood?

A zip and it is warm

title: Asking for Directions
contextVi: Một du khách hỏi người địa phương đường đến bảo tàng khoa học.

script.speaker: Tourist
script.text: Excuse me. Could you tell me how to get to the Science Museum?

script.speaker: Local
script.text: Of course. It's not far. Go straight on along this road until you reach the traffic lights.

script.speaker: Tourist
script.text: Straight on to the lights. And then?

script.speaker: Local
script.text: Turn left and walk past the post office and the bank. The museum is on your right, opposite the park.

script.speaker: Tourist
script.text: How long does it take on foot?

script.speaker: Local
script.text: About fifteen minutes. Or you can take the number twenty-two bus from the bus stop over there.

script.speaker: Tourist
script.text: Does the bus go all the way to the museum?

script.speaker: Local
script.text: Almost. You need to get off at the library, and then it's a two-minute walk.

script.speaker: Tourist
script.text: Is the museum open today?

script.speaker: Local
script.text: Yes, it's open until six. It closes at four on Sundays, but today is Saturday, so you have plenty of time.

script.speaker: Tourist
script.text: Wonderful. Thank you very much!

script.speaker: Local
script.text: You're welcome. Enjoy your visit.

questions.q: What should the tourist do at the traffic lights?
questions.explain: 'Turn left' tại đèn giao thông.

questions.q: Where is the museum?
questions.explain: 'on your right, opposite the park'.

questions.q: The walk takes about ____ minutes.
questions.explain: 'About fifteen minutes.'

questions.q: The tourist can take bus number ____.
questions.explain: 'the number twenty-two bus'.

questions.q: Where should she get off the bus?
questions.explain: 'You need to get off at the library'.

questions.q: On Sundays, the museum closes at ____ o'clock.
questions.explain: Hôm nay mở đến sáu giờ, nhưng 'It closes at four on Sundays'.

title: Planning a Birthday Party
contextVi: Hai anh em lên kế hoạch tổ chức tiệc sinh nhật cho mẹ.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: Jack, we need to plan Mum's birthday party. It's on the twentieth of June.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: That's a Saturday, isn't it? Where shall we have it?

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: I thought about a restaurant, but it's very expensive. What about at home?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Good idea. How many people are coming?

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: About twelve. Her sister, her friends from work and the neighbours. Oh, and Grandpa. So thirteen people.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: OK, thirteen. Shall we order a cake?

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: I'd rather make one myself. She likes chocolate cake best.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Wonderful. I'll do the music and the decorations. What about presents?

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: I've already bought her a scarf. Why don't we buy something together? Maybe a book about gardening?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Yes, she loves her garden. I'll order it online today.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: Thanks. The party starts at seven, but please tell everyone to come at half past six, so they are there before Mum arrives.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Good plan. I'll send messages to everyone tonight.

questions.q: The party is on the ____ of June.
questions.explain: 'It's on the twentieth of June.'

questions.q: Where will the party be?
questions.explain: Nhà hàng quá đắt nên chọn 'at home'.

questions.q: The number of guests is ____.
questions.explain: Emma nói khoảng 12 rồi cộng thêm Grandpa: 'So thirteen people.'

questions.q: What kind of cake will Emma make?
questions.explain: 'She likes chocolate cake best.'

questions.q: What will Jack do for the party?
questions.explain: Jack: 'I'll do the music and the decorations.'

questions.q: What present will they buy together?
questions.explain: Chiếc khăn là Emma đã mua riêng; quà chung là 'a book about gardening'.

questions.q: Guests should arrive at ____ (time).
questions.explain: Tiệc bắt đầu lúc bảy giờ nhưng khách đến 'half past six'.

title: Joining a Sports Centre
contextVi: Một người đàn ông gọi điện đăng ký làm thành viên phòng tập thể thao và hồ bơi.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help you?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Hi. I'd like to join the centre, please. A friend told me you have a swimming pool and a climbing wall.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: That's right. I can take your details now, if you like. What's your full name?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: It's Marcus Lindqvist.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Could you spell the surname for me?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Sure. That's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Thank you. And your address?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Forty-two Harbour Road. And the postcode is B D nine, four R T. Oh, sorry, that's wrong. It's B D nine, four R F.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: B D nine, four R F. Got it. And a contact number?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: My mobile is oh seven seven double-oh, nine double-oh, four six three.

script.text: Thank you. Now, we have two types of membership. Standard is thirty-five pounds a month and includes the gym and the pool. Premium is forty-five pounds, and it also includes classes, such as yoga and spinning.

title: A Tour of the Hartley Arts Centre
contextVi: Hướng dẫn viên giới thiệu các khu vực và quy định của một trung tâm nghệ thuật cộng đồng.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hartley Community Arts Centre. My name's Joanna, and I'll be showing you around for the next forty minutes. Before we begin, a few practical points. The centre is open from nine in the morning until nine at night every day, except Sundays, when it closes at five. Please keep your phones on silent in the galleries.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: We're standing in the main entrance hall. On your left is the café, which serves breakfast until eleven. Many people think the café is only for visitors, but it's open to everyone, and it's very popular with local artists. The cloakroom is also here, and it's free. You can leave your coats and bags, but please take any valuables with you.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Now, if you go up the main staircase, you'll find the exhibition galleries on the first floor. At the moment we have a photography exhibition about the local river, which runs until the end of November. In December, there will be a display of children's paintings from three nearby primary schools.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: On the ground floor, behind the café, are the workshop studios. We run classes in pottery, painting and printing. The pottery studio is the most popular. It was refurbished last year and now has six new kilns. You can book a taster session for ten pounds, and if you decide to join a course, that fee is taken off the price.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The small theatre is in the basement. It seats a hundred and twenty people. It was originally designed for a hundred and fifty, but the number was reduced when we added spaces for wheelchairs. There are performances most weekends, and tickets are cheaper if you buy them in advance online.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Finally, a word about volunteering. We always need helpers, especially at weekends. If you're interested, please speak to Mr Ford in the office, which is on the second floor, next to the library. Right, shall we start with the galleries? Please follow me.

questions.q: What time does the centre close on Sundays?
questions.explain: 'every day, except Sundays, when it closes at five'.

questions.q: The café serves breakfast until ____ o'clock.
questions.explain: 'serves breakfast until eleven'.

questions.q: What is the current photography exhibition about?
questions.explain: 'a photography exhibition about the local river'; tranh thiếu nhi là triển lãm tháng 12.

questions.q: The pottery studio has six new ____.
questions.explain: 'now has six new kilns'.

questions.q: A taster session costs £____.
questions.explain: 'book a taster session for ten pounds'.

questions.q: How many people does the theatre seat now?
questions.explain: Ban đầu thiết kế 150 chỗ, nhưng hiện 'seats a hundred and twenty' vì thêm chỗ cho xe lăn.

questions.q: People who want to volunteer should speak to Mr ____.
questions.explain: 'please speak to Mr Ford in the office'.

title: How to Use GreenWheels Bike Hire
contextVi: Bản ghi âm hướng dẫn cách sử dụng dịch vụ thuê xe đạp công cộng trong thành phố.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Welcome to GreenWheels, the city's bike-hire scheme. In this recording, we explain how to use our service. There are two hundred bikes available at forty stations across the city. To use the bikes, you first need to download the GreenWheels app. Registration takes about two minutes, and you'll need a credit or debit card. We ask for a deposit of twenty pounds, which is returned when you close your account.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: Now, the prices. The first thirty minutes of every journey are free. After that, the charge is one pound for each additional thirty minutes. For longer trips, the day pass costs five pounds. Sorry, that's the old price. The day pass now costs six pounds, and it allows unlimited journeys of up to ninety minutes each. The weekly pass costs fifteen pounds.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: To unlock a bike, scan the QR code on the handlebars with your phone. The bikes have built-in lights and a basket at the front. Helmets are not provided, but you can buy one for eight pounds at the information point in Central Station.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: You can return a bike to any station. If the station is full, press the help button on the dock, and you will receive an extra fifteen minutes free. The most popular stations are at the railway station and the university, so they are often empty in the morning and full in the evening. To solve this, our vans move bikes between stations during the day, and you can check which stations have free bikes on the app map.

script.speaker: Announcer
script.text: A few safety tips. Please use cycle lanes where possible, and remember that it is illegal to cycle on pavements. If a bike is damaged, press report in the app, lock the bike, and choose another one. For further help, call our customer service line, which is open from seven in the morning until ten at night.

questions.q: How many stations does the scheme have?
questions.explain: 'two hundred bikes available at forty stations'.

questions.q: Users pay a deposit of £____.
questions.explain: 'a deposit of twenty pounds'.

questions.q: The first ____ minutes of each journey are free.
questions.explain: 'The first thirty minutes of every journey are free.'

questions.q: The day pass costs £____ now.
questions.explain: Người nói sửa: giá cũ là 5 bảng, 'now costs six pounds'.

questions.q: How do users unlock a bike?

title: Planning a Survey on Student Sleep
contextVi: Hai sinh viên tâm lý học thảo luận với giảng viên về kế hoạch khảo sát thói quen ngủ của sinh viên năm nhất.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your psychology project on student sleep.

script.speaker: Chloe
script.text: Yes. We've decided to carry out a survey of first-year students, asking how many hours they sleep and how it affects their concentration.

script.speaker: Ravi
script.text: We originally planned to interview about fifty people face to face, but we realised it would take far too long, so we're going to use an online questionnaire instead.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: That seems sensible. How many responses are you hoping to get?

script.speaker: Chloe
script.text: At least a hundred and twenty. Anything less wouldn't give us reliable results.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Good. But be careful with the length. If the questionnaire is too long, people will give up halfway.

script.speaker: Ravi
script.text: We've limited it to fifteen questions. We thought about adding questions on diet and exercise too, but Chloe thinks that would make the project too broad.

script.speaker: Chloe
script.text: Right. We'll concentrate on sleep duration, bedtime and phone use.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Sensible again. Now, how will you measure concentration? Self-reporting can be unreliable.

script.speaker: Ravi
script.text: We thought of a short memory test at the end. Participants see twenty words for one minute, then write down as many as they can remember.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: That's a nice idea, but think about timing. If people do it late in the evening, when they're already tired, the results will be affected whatever their sleep was like.

script.speaker: Chloe
script.text: Good point. We'll ask them to complete it in the morning, then.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Also, think about ethics. You must include a consent statement at the start, and the responses have to be anonymous.

script.speaker: Ravi
script.text: Yes, we'll make sure that no names are collected. For the analysis, Doctor Patel recommended a statistics program that's free to download, so we'll try that rather than a spreadsheet.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Good. Now, the final report is due on the twelfth of December, but I'd like to see a draft of your method section by the end of October.

script.speaker: Chloe
script.text: That's fine. And the presentation?

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Ten minutes, with five minutes for questions. I suggest you include a graph showing hours of sleep against test score. It will make your argument much clearer.

script.speaker: Ravi
script.text: We'll do that. Thank you very much.

title: A Marketing Plan for a Bookshop Café
contextVi: Hai sinh viên marketing trình bày với giảng viên kế hoạch thu hút khách cho một quán cà phê sách.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Right, let's go through your marketing project. You chose the bookshop café on Elm Street, didn't you?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Yes. The owner told us that the main problem is that business is slow on weekday afternoons, so our target group is students.

script.speaker: Omar
script.text: We visited three times last week and counted the customers. Between two and five o'clock, there were never more than eight people in the café, compared with over thirty at weekends.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: That's useful evidence. What solutions are you proposing?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Our first idea was a loyalty card, where you buy nine coffees and get the tenth free. But the owner said that a rival café nearby already does that, so we dropped it.

script.speaker: Omar
script.text: Instead, we're proposing a study hour. Students who buy a drink can stay and use a quiet area with free Wi-Fi.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Hmm, there's a risk there. Students might occupy tables for hours after buying just one coffee.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We thought of that. We suggest a limit of three hours per drink, and the quiet area would be upstairs, which is hardly ever used.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Good. And how will you promote it?

script.speaker: Omar
script.text: We were going to print leaflets, but our survey of forty students showed that most of them would never read them. They said they follow local businesses on Instagram.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: So we'll make a short video of the quiet area and post it online.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: What about the budget?

script.speaker: Omar
script.text: The owner can spare two hundred pounds. The leaflets would have cost seventy, but now we'll use the money for coffee vouchers for the first week, and to pay a student to make the video.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Fine. How will you evaluate whether it works?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We'll count the customers on weekday afternoons for four weeks and compare them with our first figures.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Be careful, though. Student numbers are strongly affected by exams. If your four weeks fall during the exam period, the results could be misleading.

script.speaker: Omar
script.text: Then we'll start the trial in the third week of term, not at the end.

script.speaker: Mr Davies
script.text: Excellent. One last thing. The written report should be two and a half thousand words, plus appendices.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Two and a half thousand. Thanks very much.

title: A Waste Audit of the Campus Canteen
contextVi: Hai sinh viên khoa học môi trường báo cáo kết quả kiểm kê rác ở căng-tin và bàn kế hoạch tiếp theo với giảng viên.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: So, James, Priya, your waste audit. Tell me where you are.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We've finished the first stage. We weighed all the waste from the main canteen for five days, starting on the second of March.

script.speaker: James
script.text: The total was about four hundred kilograms. Roughly a third of that was food waste, around forty percent was paper and cardboard, fifteen percent was plastic, and the rest was mixed waste.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: A third is lower than I'd expect. Canteen waste is usually closer to half food.

script.speaker: James
script.text: We wondered about that. That week there was a field trip, so many students weren't on campus.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Then your figures may not be typical. I'd repeat the measurement in a normal week, at least for food waste.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Okay, we can do that. The real problem we noticed is the mixed waste. A lot of recyclable material goes into general bins, and when different types are mixed, the recycling company rejects the whole load.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That's called contamination, and it's a common problem. Why do you think it happens?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We interviewed thirty students, and most of them weren't sure which bin to use. The labels are small and just use words.

script.speaker: James
script.text: So we propose clearer signs with pictures, and colour coding for each bin. We also thought about a reusable cup scheme with a deposit of one pound.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: It's fifty pence in our proposal, remember? A pound would put students off.

script.speaker: James
script.text: Right, fifty pence.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: The cup scheme is a good idea, but you only have a few weeks, so I'd concentrate on the signs. Could you test them on two floors of the building and count the contamination before and after?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We'd love to, but the facilities manager has to approve it first.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Send her an email this week and copy me in. How do you plan to present the results?

script.speaker: James
script.text: A pie chart for the composition of the waste, and a bar chart comparing the before and after figures.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Good. Remember the assessment is a poster presentation on the fourth of May, not a written report. Keep the text short.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Understood. Thank you, Dr Okafor.

title: Preparing a Seminar on the Silk Road
contextVi: Hai sinh viên lịch sử trao đổi với giảng viên về bài thuyết trình hội thảo về Con đường Tơ lụa.

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: Let's discuss your seminar presentation on the Silk Road. Have you decided on a focus?

script.speaker: Leila
script.text: We started with the idea of covering the whole route, from China to the Mediterranean, but that was far too broad. We've narrowed it down to the exchange of goods and ideas in Central Asia, especially in the city of Samarkand.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Samarkand was a real crossroads. We want to show that the Silk Road was about ideas as much as silk. Religion, technology, even paper-making.

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: Good. Paper is a lovely example. Chinese paper-making reached Samarkand in the eighth century, and from there it spread west to the Islamic world and eventually to Europe.

script.speaker: Leila
script.text: We'd like to include that. We've also found a primary source, a translation of the diary of a Chinese monk who travelled through the region.

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: Excellent. But remember that travellers' accounts can be biased, so you should say who he was writing for.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Should we organise the talk chronologically, starting from the earliest trade?

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: I'd suggest a thematic structure instead: trade goods, religion and technology. A chronological talk often turns into a list of dates.

script.speaker: Leila
script.text: That makes sense. Three sections, then.

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: And make sure that your sources include at least two academic books, and not only websites.

script.speaker: Tom

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: Then request an inter-library loan. It usually takes about a week, so do it today.

script.speaker: Leila
script.text: We will. What about visual aids?

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: Use a map to show the routes, but avoid long text on your slides. No more than six lines per slide.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: How long should the presentation be? And it's on the nineteenth of November, isn't it?

script.speaker: Dr Mason
script.text: Twenty minutes, followed by a short discussion. And actually, the seminar has been moved a week earlier, to the twelfth of November.

title: Lecture: Urban Heat Islands
contextVi: Bài giảng đại học về hiện tượng đảo nhiệt đô thị, nguyên nhân, hậu quả và các giải pháp.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at a phenomenon that affects most large cities: the urban heat island. This is the observation that the centre of a city is often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, particularly at night. In a city of a million people, the difference in average annual temperature can be between one and three degrees Celsius, but on a calm, clear evening the gap can reach as much as twelve degrees.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Why does this happen? There are three main causes. The first is the materials used in construction. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roof tiles absorb a great deal of solar radiation during the day, and release it slowly after sunset, so cities cool down far less quickly than rural areas. The second cause is the loss of vegetation. Plants cool the air through a process called evapotranspiration, in which water evaporates from their leaves, and when plants are replaced by concrete, this natural air conditioning disappears. The third cause is waste heat. Vehicles, air conditioners and industry all release heat directly into the air. And we should add the geometry of cities. Tall buildings trap heat between them, and they block the winds that would otherwise carry it away.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The consequences are more serious than simple discomfort. Heat waves are already the deadliest weather events in many countries, and the heat island effect makes them worse, especially at night, when the body would normally recover. Elderly people, and those living alone on the upper floors of poorly ventilated buildings, are most at risk. In addition, hotter cities use more electricity for cooling, and this creates a vicious circle. The extra energy often comes from fossil fuels, which add to global warming, and the air conditioners themselves expel more heat into the street.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So, what can be done? Three strategies have been widely studied. The first is increasing reflectivity. Painting roofs white, or using light-coloured paving, can reduce surface temperatures significantly. The drawback is that in winter, reflective surfaces prevent buildings from absorbing useful warmth. In cities with long, hot summers, though, the balance is clearly positive.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The second strategy is greening: planting trees, creating parks and installing green roofs. Trees offer both shade and evapotranspiration, and studies suggest that neighbourhoods with thirty percent tree cover can be up to four degrees cooler than those without. Green roofs, which are planted with grasses or other shallow-rooted plants, also absorb rainwater, which helps to reduce flooding. However, they are expensive to install and need maintenance, so they are more common on public buildings than on private homes.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The third approach involves urban design. Planners can leave open corridors so that breezes can reach the city centre, and avoid dense blocks that trap heat. Some cities, such as Stuttgart in Germany, have mapped the routes of cold air flowing down from the surrounding hills, and they prohibit building along them. Whichever approach is chosen, research shows that the benefits are greatest when several methods are combined, and when they are targeted at the neighbourhoods that are hottest and poorest, since wealthier areas typically already have more trees.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: In next week's session, we'll look at how these strategies were evaluated in three case studies. Before that, please read the two articles on the course website.

questions.explain: 'Elderly people, and those living alone on the upper floors of poorly ventilated buildings, are most at risk.'

title: Lecture: The Psychology of Habit
contextVi: Bài giảng về cách thói quen hình thành trong não bộ và những chiến lược xây dựng hoặc bỏ thói quen.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Welcome to today's lecture on the psychology of habit. Let me begin with a statistic. Researchers at Duke University estimated that around forty percent of our daily actions are performed not because we have consciously decided to do them, but out of habit. We brush our teeth, drive to work and reach for our phones, often without any conscious thought at all.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So what is a habit? It's a behaviour that is triggered automatically by a context. Neuroscientists have located habit in a group of structures deep in the brain called the basal ganglia. When a behaviour is new, the prefrontal cortex is heavily involved, and the task demands effort and attention. As the behaviour is repeated, control passes to the basal ganglia, which frees the prefrontal cortex for other tasks. This explains why an experienced driver can hold a conversation while changing gear.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The most influential model describes a habit loop with three components: a cue, a routine and a reward. The cue might be a time of day, a place, an emotion, or the presence of particular people. The routine is the behaviour itself. The reward is the benefit that reinforces the loop, so that next time the cue appears, the craving for the reward starts before the behaviour does. Take the example of afternoon snacking. The cue might be a drop in energy at three o'clock, and the routine is walking to the vending machine. But the reward might not be the food at all. It might be a short break and a chat with colleagues. This matters, because if you want to change a habit, you must identify the real reward.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: How long does it take to form a habit? You'll often hear that it takes twenty-one days. That number has no scientific basis. It comes from an observation made by a plastic surgeon in the nineteen sixties, about how long his patients took to get used to their new appearance. A study at University College London asked participants to adopt a simple new behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water after breakfast. The average time before the behaviour became automatic was sixty-six days, but the range was enormous, from eighteen days to two hundred and fifty-four. More complicated behaviours, such as doing fifty sit-ups, took longer than simple ones. Interestingly, missing a single day did not seriously damage the process.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Based on this research, three strategies are particularly effective. First, make the new behaviour small. Rather than aiming to run five kilometres, start by simply putting on your running shoes. Second, attach the new behaviour to an existing cue, for example: after I pour my morning coffee, I will write one sentence in my journal. Third, change the environment. If you want to eat fewer biscuits, don't rely on willpower alone; put them in a cupboard that's hard to reach. Studies in cafeterias show that simply moving healthy food to eye level significantly increases the number of people who choose it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Breaking bad habits is harder, because the link between cue and routine remains in the brain even after we stop. That's why relapses are common during periods of stress, when the prefrontal cortex is less effective. The most successful approach is usually replacement rather than suppression. Keep the cue and the reward, but swap the routine. A smoker who always had a cigarette during a work break might go for a short walk instead.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: For next week's seminar, please bring one habit you would like to change, and try to analyse its cue and its reward. That's all for today.

questions.explain: 'around forty percent of our daily actions are performed ... out of habit'.

questions.explain: 'control passes to the basal ganglia'.

options: It did not seriously damage the process
questions.explain: 'missing a single day did not seriously damage the process'.

questions.explain: 'moving healthy food to eye level'.

title: Lecture: The Decline of Pollinators
contextVi: Bài giảng về vai trò của côn trùng thụ phấn, nguyên nhân suy giảm và các giải pháp.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today's lecture is about pollinators, and why their decline has attracted so much attention from scientists, farmers and governments. Roughly three quarters of the world's major food crops depend, at least in part, on animal pollination, and the annual value of this service has been estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Pollinators include bees, but also hoverflies, butterflies, moths and beetles, and in some regions even bats and birds.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Bees themselves are far more diverse than most people realise. Of around twenty thousand species worldwide, only a handful, including the western honey bee, live in large colonies and are managed by beekeepers. The vast majority are solitary bees, in which each female builds her own nest, often in bare soil or in hollow stems. Many wild bees are more efficient pollinators than honey bees. For instance, bumblebees can perform what's called buzz pollination. By vibrating their flight muscles, they shake pollen out of flowers such as tomatoes and blueberries, something honey bees cannot do.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Evidence for decline is strongest in Europe and North America. A study in Germany found that the total mass of flying insects in protected areas fell by more than seventy percent over twenty-seven years. In the United Kingdom, several species of bumblebee have disappeared from large parts of their former range. Honey bees are a more complicated case. The global number of managed hives has actually risen, but beekeepers in some countries report high winter losses.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: What is causing the decline? Researchers talk about a combination of pressures. The first, and probably the most important, is habitat loss. Intensive farming has removed hedgerows and meadows, leaving bees with fewer flowers and fewer nesting sites. The second is pesticides. Neonicotinoids, a class of insecticide, do not usually kill bees directly at normal doses, but studies indicate that they impair navigation and reduce reproduction. The European Union restricted the outdoor use of three of these chemicals in two thousand and thirteen, and later extended the ban. The third pressure is disease and parasites, notably the varroa mite, which feeds on honey bees and spreads viruses. And finally, climate change is disrupting timing. Flowers may bloom earlier than the bees emerge, a problem known as phenological mismatch.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Crucially, these pressures interact. A colony weakened by poor nutrition is less able to resist parasites, and a bee exposed to a small dose of pesticide is more likely to get lost on a flight. That's why studying one factor in isolation can be misleading.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: What about solutions? At the farm level, sowing strips of wildflowers along field edges has proved effective in several experiments. In cities, rooftop gardens, parks and even road verges can provide food, if gardeners choose a variety of flowers that bloom throughout the season, rather than showy hybrids that produce little nectar. And policy matters too: reducing pesticide use, and paying farmers for conservation.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: One word of caution about a popular response, which is to keep honey bees in the city. Setting up hives may be good for honey production, but if too many hives compete for the same flowers, they can reduce the food available to wild bees. So, in many cases, planting flowers is more useful than keeping hives.

title: Lecture: The Printing Press Revolution
contextVi: Bài giảng lịch sử về sự ra đời của máy in và các tranh luận về tác động của nó tới châu Âu.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: In today's lecture, I'd like to examine the invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century, and to ask a question that historians continue to debate: was it a revolution, or a gradual evolution? Let's begin with what existed before. In medieval Europe, books were copied by hand, mostly by monks in monasteries, and a single Bible might take a scribe more than a year to complete. Books were therefore very expensive. A university might own only a few hundred, and many were chained to desks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Printing with movable type was not new in itself. It had been used in China and Korea centuries earlier, and the earliest surviving book printed with metal type is a Korean Buddhist text from thirteen seventy-seven. What Johannes Gutenberg, working in Mainz around fourteen fifty, contributed was a combination of technologies: a metal alloy that could be cast into durable, identical letters, an oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and a press adapted from those used for making wine. Why did it succeed in Europe? Partly because the alphabet has few characters, so it's practical to cast a full set of letters, whereas Chinese writing needs thousands of different characters.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The speed at which printing spread was remarkable. By fifteen hundred, presses had been set up in more than two hundred cities, and some historians estimate that between ten and twenty million books had been printed. The price of books fell dramatically, by about two thirds in the first fifty years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: What were the consequences? The most obvious is the spread of ideas. Martin Luther's ninety-five theses of fifteen seventeen spread across Germany in a matter of weeks, and his pamphlets sold in hundreds of thousands, helping to transform a theological dispute into the Reformation. In science, printing allowed researchers to share and compare data accurately. Copernicus's work, and later Vesalius's anatomical illustrations, could be reproduced consistently, something impossible when each copyist introduced new errors. The historian Elizabeth Eisenstein argued, in nineteen seventy-nine, that this fixity of text was the foundation of modern science.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: But there are other views. Some scholars argue that Eisenstein exaggerates. Early printed books also contained errors, and censorship appeared quickly. The Church published a list of prohibited books in the sixteenth century. Moreover, literacy rates increased only slowly. In fifteen hundred, probably no more than ten percent of adults in Europe could read. Printing, these critics say, strengthened trends that were already under way, rather than creating them. And there's an economic dimension. Printers were businessmen who published what would sell, which meant popular works such as almanacs, romances and religious tracts, as well as scholarly texts in Latin.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Gutenberg himself, incidentally, did not prosper. He borrowed heavily to finance his Bible project, lost a lawsuit to his financial partner, and had to hand over his equipment. Nobody knows exactly how many copies of his Bible were printed. The usual estimate is about one hundred and eighty, of which forty-nine survive in whole or in part.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Next week, we'll look at some interesting parallels between the printing press and the arrival of the internet. Please read the chapter on information technology before then.
